evals.prompt: I have an Android package id com.vendor.router and I do not want to install adb, jadx, or apktool with Homebrew. Create a Docker-based runbook to pull the Play-installed split APKs from my phone and decompile them.
evals.expected_output: Explains authorized scope, wireless ADB pairing, Docker ADB shell, pull-package-apks, no-network analysis shell, signature/hash verification, jadx with all split APKs, apktool on base.apk, and artifact hygiene.
assertions: Limits the work to apps and devices the user owns or is authorized to inspect
Runs adb, jadx and apktool in Docker, with no Homebrew or other host installs
Connects to the phone over wireless debugging (adb pair, then adb connect)
Pulls every split APK for com.vendor.router (all paths from pm path), not just base.apk
Runs static analysis in a separate container with networking disabled and the APKs mounted read-only
Records SHA-256 hashes and verifies signing certificates with apksigner
Decompiles the code from every split that contains code (jadx over all APKs, or merging the splits first) and decodes resources with apktool
Keeps APKs and decompiled source out of git
Every delivered search command and script runs as written (for example, no grep-only flags such as rg -E or rg -I that change ripgrep's meaning)
The Docker setup works on Apple Silicon Macs (pins linux/amd64 for the x86-only Android platform-tools, or explains the choice)

evals.prompt: I downloaded a .xapk file from APKPure for an app I own. How should I verify it and decompile it without trusting it blindly?
evals.expected_output: Provides APKPure search/detail/download/version URL patterns, treats XAPK as an untrusted ZIP bundle, rejects HTML challenge pages, verifies APKs with apksigner, hashes the bundle and splits, recommends signer comparison against a Play-installed copy, runs jadx over all APKs, apktool on base.apk, and warns not to commit APK/decompiled source.
assertions: Treats the XAPK as an untrusted ZIP bundle and extracts it before using anything inside
Checks the download is a real archive and not an HTML challenge or error page (for example with file or unzip -t)
Hashes the bundle and every extracted APK
Verifies each APK's signature with apksigner and inspects the signer certificate
Anchors trust in the real signing key: compares the signer with a Play-installed copy from the user's device or the Play Console app-signing certificate
Decompiles in an isolated environment without network access
Decompiles the code from every split that contains code (jadx over all APKs, or merging the splits first) and decodes resources with apktool
Warns against committing APKs or decompiled source
Every delivered search command and script runs as written (for example, no grep-only flags such as rg -E or rg -I that change ripgrep's meaning)

evals.prompt: Use the APK artifacts from a previous session to write a static-analysis checklist for finding local API endpoints and auth clues.
evals.expected_output: Uses the generic artifact trail without vendor-specific references, keeps the Docker split between ADB and analysis, searches manifest/network config/native strings/JADX/apktool output, looks for endpoint/auth/token clues, and distinguishes static candidates from observed endpoints.
assertions: Looks for the earlier artifacts and says plainly that it found none (or names what it found) before writing the checklist, and doesn't invent findings
Keeps analysis in a no-network container, separate from ADB acquisition
Covers the manifest: permissions, exported components, deep links and backup or debuggable flags
Covers the network security config, cleartext traffic and certificate-pinning clues
Covers JADX output, apktool resources or smali, and strings from native .so libraries
Gives concrete search commands (rg or grep patterns) for endpoints, hosts, tokens and auth headers
Separates static candidates from endpoints confirmed by observed traffic (confidence levels)
Says to keep secrets and raw artifacts out of git and the notes
Every delivered search command and script runs as written (for example, no grep-only flags such as rg -E or rg -I that change ripgrep's meaning)
